message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Market Analysis: Launching a Digital Subscription for the Calderbrook Courier
Commercial Strategy, Calderbrook Media, April 2026

1. Purpose
The Calderbrook Courier's website is free to read and funded by display advertising, which has declined by about 12% a year for three years. This paper assesses the market for a metered digital subscription, in which readers can view five articles a month free before being asked to subscribe, and recommends a price and launch plan.

2. Our audience
The website had an average of 420,000 monthly unique users (MUU) in 2025, of whom around 60% live in the Courier's circulation area. The printed Courier has 11,200 subscribers paying £18.50 a month for six-day home delivery, plus around 6,000 daily news-stand sales. Print subscribers are older on average than web readers, and most also use the website.

In our March 2026 survey of print subscribers (1,850 responses), 30% said they would cancel their print subscription and take a digital-only subscription instead if one were offered at under £6 a month.

3. Evidence from comparable titles
We obtained data, under confidentiality agreements, from four regional titles that launched metered subscriptions between 2022 and 2024.

Table 1. Comparable regional titles, second year after launch
Title | Monthly unique users | Digital subscribers | Subscribers as % of MUU | Monthly price
Title A | 360,000 | 6,800 | 1.9% | £5.99
Title B | 280,000 | 3,100 | 1.1% | £4.99
Title C | 390,000 | 9,400 | 2.4% | £7.99
Title D | 300,000 | 4,200 | 1.4% | £3.99

All four titles reported that subscriber numbers stabilised by the end of the second year, and that churn settled at between 3% and 5% a month after promotional periods ended.

4. Price
Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices, which suggests that our audience will respond best to a low price point. We therefore propose a price of £4.99 a month, with an introductory offer of £1 for the first three months.

5. Projection
The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU. Applied to our 420,000 MUU, that gives about 8,400 subscribers by the end of year two. At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue.

Table 2. Year-two projection
Item | Annual amount
Subscription revenue | £503,000
Subscription platform and payment fees | £85,000
Marketing | £60,000
Net contribution | £358,000

We expect a modest reduction in display advertising revenue as page views from non-subscribers fall when they reach the meter; the comparable titles reported falls of 5% to 8% in page views. Our display revenue was £1.1 million in 2025, so a fall of this size would cost between £55,000 and £88,000 a year, which is well covered by the projected net contribution.

6. Launch plan
- Platform selection and integration: May to July 2026.
- Soft launch with a ten-article meter: September 2026.
- Full launch with a five-article meter: November 2026.
- Review of price and meter after six months.

7. Conclusion
The evidence from comparable titles shows a viable market for a Courier digital subscription. At £4.99 a month, a price that the comparable titles' experience suggests will maximise take-up, we project around 8,400 subscribers and a net contribution of £358,000 a year, more than offsetting the expected effect on display advertising. We recommend approval to proceed with the launch plan.
</document>
response:
# Review: Market Analysis for a Courier Digital Subscription

The paper is clearly structured, but its recommendation rests on a misreading of Table 1, an arithmetic error, and the omission of print cannibalisation. Once these are corrected, the case for launching at £4.99 looks considerably weaker, and possibly loss-making. The issues are listed in order of importance.

## Major issues

**1. The pricing rationale contradicts the paper's own data (Section 4).**
The paper says conversion is highest at the lowest prices. Table 1 shows otherwise:

| Price | Title | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| £3.99 | D | 1.4% |
| £4.99 | B | 1.1% (lowest) |
| £5.99 | A | 1.9% |
| £7.99 | C | 2.4% (highest) |

If anything, the relationship runs the other way, although four titles are too few to support any conclusion about price. The proposed £4.99 matches the comparable with the *worst* conversion. Conclusion 7 repeats the claim that this price "will maximise take-up," which is also unsupported. The section needs to be rewritten. It should also consider whether a higher price would yield more revenue.

**2. The average conversion rate is wrong (Section 5).**
The mean of 1.9%, 1.1%, 2.4% and 1.4% is **1.7%**, not 2.0%. The pooled rate (23,500 subscribers ÷ 1.33m MUU) is 1.77%.

| Scenario | Subscribers | Revenue | Net contribution (after £145k costs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paper (2.0%) | 8,400 | £503k | £358k |
| Corrected average (1.7%) | 7,140 | £428k | £283k |
| Title B rate (1.1%, same price) | 4,620 | £277k | £132k |

**3. Print cannibalisation is ignored, and it may outweigh the entire projected gain.**
Section 2 reports that 30% of surveyed print subscribers would switch to digital-only below £6, which includes the proposed £4.99. Applied to 11,200 subscribers, that is about 3,360 switching from £18.50 to £4.99:

> 3,360 × (£18.50 − £4.99) × 12 ≈ **£545,000 a year in lost print revenue**

This exceeds even the paper's own £358k net contribution. Two further points follow from it:
- The switchers would probably make up a large share of the projected digital subscribers. That means the *incremental* digital revenue is lower still.
- Print production and delivery savings would partly offset the loss, but they are not quantified.

The survey figure has limitations. Respondents may not represent all subscribers, and stated intentions often overstate actual behaviour. Even so, the paper cannot report this finding and then leave it out of the financials. Mitigations to assess include a print+digital bundle, a digital price closer to £6 or above, and keeping digital-only offers away from existing print subscribers.

## Moderate issues

**4. The year-two revenue treats the end-of-year subscriber count as a full-year average.** The comparables only "stabilised by the end of the second year," so average subscribers during year two will be lower than 8,400.

**5. Churn and acquisition costs are not modelled.** Monthly churn of 3–5% means losing roughly 30–45% of subscribers a year. Holding a steady base requires continual acquisition. It is unclear whether £60k of marketing can achieve this. The £1 introductory offer also drags on revenue, and post-promotion drop-off is not addressed.

**6. The comparability of the audiences is not established.** The Courier's MUU (420k) is higher than all four comparables. Only 60% of its users are local, and out-of-area readers usually convert poorly. The paper does not give the comparables' local share or meter settings. Without them, applying their conversion rates to the Courier's total MUU may overstate the result.

**7. Ad revenue impact.** The 5–8% calculation (£55k–£88k) is arithmetically correct. However, the conclusion that it is "well covered" depends on the overstated contribution. Under the corrected scenarios, plus cannibalisation, it is not covered. The paper should also be clear that this loss comes on top of the existing ~12% annual decline in display revenue.

## Minor points

- **Platform fees:** £85k is about 17% of revenue. The paper should state whether this is fixed or variable, since that affects the downside scenarios.
- **Timeline:** The paper is dated April 2026, and the plan scheduled full launch for November 2026, which is now. If this is still awaiting approval, Section 6 needs new dates. If the launch has gone ahead, the soft-launch data from September should replace the comparables-based projections.
- **Sample size:** Four comparables is a small sample. The paper should present projections as a range (low/central/high), not a single point estimate.

## Suggested revisions

1. Rewrite Section 4. Either remove the price–conversion claim or test several price points, including £5.99–£7.99.
2. Correct the average to 1.7% and present a range of scenarios.
3. Add a print cannibalisation line to Table 2, net of print cost savings, and consider bundle pricing.
4. Model a subscriber ramp, churn and the introductory-offer period, not a single steady-state year.
5. Revise the conclusion so it follows from the corrected figures.

As it stands, the evidence does not support the claim that a £4.99 subscription would more than offset its costs. The recommendation should not be approved until the projection is reworked.
